stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Dietary fiber slows the rate at which sugar enters the bloodstream. Oats, beans, and lentils are especially rich in soluble fiber, a type of fiber that forms a thick gel inside the digestive tract. This gel traps some of the sugar from a meal, ______ the sharp rise in blood glucose that often follows eating.
explanation: The last sentence already has a subject (this gel) and a main verb (traps). Nothing after the comma joins on another clause: there is no 'and', no 'which', no 'that'. So the blank can only begin a descriptive add-on, and 'reducing' does that job. It describes what the trapping does. This is the one step under every question where the blank follows a complete clause and a comma: count the main verbs first. If the subject already has one, the blank needs a participle.

B.why: 'Reduces' is a second tensed verb with nothing joining it to 'traps'. You read 'reduces' as fine on its own and didn't notice the sentence already had its main verb. It would only work with 'and' in front of it.

C.why: 'It reduces' is a complete independent clause, so placing it after a comma creates a comma splice. You probably chose it because it sounds like a full, careful sentence, but two full sentences can't be joined by a comma alone.

D.why: Here 'reduced' acts as a past-tense main verb with an object ('the sharp rise'), so it adds a second finite verb and also clashes with the present tense of 'traps'. You may have reached for '-ed' because it looks like a modifier, but '-ed' only describes a noun that receives an action. The gel is doing the reducing, so the form has to be '-ing'.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Many farmers now plant clover in their fields after the autumn harvest. Over the winter, the clover covers the bare ground and keeps rain from washing the topsoil away. In spring, the clover is tilled back into the soil, ______ by microbes into nitrogen that the next crop can absorb.
explanation: The last sentence already has its subject (the clover) and its main verb (is tilled). The blank begins an add-on that describes the clover, so it must be a participle and not another tensed verb. The clover receives the action: microbes break it down, as 'by microbes' shows. That calls for the '-ed' form, 'broken down'. Deciding between '-ed' and '-ing' this way is the second half of every supplementary-phrase question on the test.

A.why: 'Is broken down' is a full passive verb. Putting it after the comma gives the sentence two main verbs with no 'and' between them. It looks correct because it matches 'is tilled', but matching isn't enough without a connecting word.

C.why: 'Was broken down' adds a second main verb with no conjunction, and it also moves into the past tense while the rest of the passage is in the present. You chose a form that sounds grammatical by itself without counting the verbs already in the sentence.

D.why: You correctly saw that the blank needs a participle, but you picked the wrong one. '-ing' means the noun does the action. The clover doesn't break anything down; microbes break the clover down. 'By microbes' marks the clover as the receiver, so '-ed' is required.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Before the late 1700s, no single machine could spin cotton thread that was both fine and strong. The spinning mule, ______ by the English weaver Samuel Crompton in 1779, combined the moving carriage of one earlier machine with the rollers of another. Within a few decades, mills across northern England had adopted it.
explanation: The subject is 'the spinning mule', and its main verb, 'combined', comes after the second comma. The part between the commas is an add-on describing the mule, so it can't contain a tensed verb. The mule was invented by Crompton, so it receives the action and the '-ed' form fits: 'invented'. This trains the habit you need when an interrupter separates a subject from its verb: find the real main verb before filling the gap.

A.why: With 'was invented', 'the spinning mule was invented' becomes a full clause. Then 'combined' has no subject and is left hanging. You treated the blank as the main verb because you didn't look past the comma, where the real main verb was waiting.

B.why: 'It was invented' drops a complete clause into the middle of the sentence, and the second 'it' repeats the mule. You chose a complete sentence where only a describing phrase can go.

D.why: You saw that a participle was needed, but '-ing' would mean the mule did the inventing. 'By ... Samuel Crompton' shows that the mule was invented, so the receiving form '-ed' is required.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In much Baroque music, the keyboard part was not written out note by note. Composers gave the player only a bass line with small numbers printed beneath it, a system known as figured bass. The keyboardist read those numbers as instructions for chords, ______ the harmony above the written bass line during performance.
explanation: The last sentence already has a subject (the keyboardist) and a main verb (read). The blank begins an add-on that describes what the keyboardist did while reading the numbers, so it needs a participle. The keyboardist performs the action, which calls for the '-ing' form: 'filling in'. Recognising that a sentence is already complete before the comma lets you answer the test's 'participle in a supplementary phrase' questions in one step.

A.why: 'They filled in' is a complete independent clause joined by a comma alone, which is a comma splice. 'They' also doesn't match the singular 'keyboardist'. You chose a full sentence where only a describing phrase can go.

B.why: 'Fills in' is a second tensed verb with no 'and', and it is in the present tense while 'read' is past. You looked at the blank on its own and didn't check the verb already doing the work.

D.why: With an object after it ('the harmony'), 'filled in' works as a past-tense main verb. That gives the sentence two main verbs with nothing joining them. It may have looked right because it matches the tense of 'read', but matching tense doesn't make a second main verb legal without 'and'.
